docs.title: 🔐 Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Edge Security: No service is exposed via plain HTTP. All traffic is TLS-encrypted.
  • Identity: We use a "Zero Trust" approach: services without their own OIDC login sit behind a forward-auth AuthWall, which checks the OIDC session before traffic reaches the service (see Lab authentication). Our own software (AmCAT, AnnoTinder) follows the Authentication standard.
  • 2FA: Multi-factor authentication is required for all researcher logins via the lab OIDC provider.
  • Resilience: All servers perform daily off-site backups to the University NAS.

docs.title: Browser authenticates with OIDC
docs.text:
Browser session authentication is managed by an OIDC provider capable of handling enterprise and institutional security requirements. The OIDC provider only does authentication: letting users securely prove to AmCAT that they own an email address.

For University hosted AmCAT servers we recommend the institution's own identity provider. See the Authentication standard for the requirements, and the Installation guide for choosing a provider.

    OIDC -->|2. JWT w/ 2FA Claim| Backend
    Backend -->|3. http-only cookie with JWTs|User

docs.title: Infrastructure Details
docs.text:
• Proxy: Caddy serving on Port 443.
  • Frontend: Vite-built React SPA served at /.
  • Backend API: FastAPI server mounted at /api.
  • OIDC flow: Initiated and callback on Backend; tokens set as signed, http-only session cookie
  • Data Storage (ES): ElasticSearch, used for both metadata and primary textual data storage.
  • Object Storage (S3): S3-compatible storage for large files.
  • Deployment Note: FastAPI, ElasticSearch, and S3 are decoupled and may reside on different physical or virtual servers.

docs.title: Two-factor authentication: where should it live?
docs.text:
All our software requires a second factor (2FA, MFA) for sensitive actions (see the Authentication standard). This page discusses which component provides that second factor: the OIDC provider (option A), or a component of our own (option B). It explains the relevant concepts, lists the pros and cons of both options, and ends with a recommendation.

This page is about AmCAT and AnnoTinder, including when other teams host them. The lab's own infrastructure is discussed in Lab authentication.

docs.title: Authentication factors
docs.text:
A factor is a type of proof that you are who you claim to be: something you know (password), something you have (phone, security key, access to an inbox), or something you are (fingerprint, usually used to unlock a device). Two-factor authentication means that a login requires two different types of proof, so that stealing one is not enough.

Two things are easy to overlook:

  • Email is a factor. Logging in via an email link, or via an account whose password can be reset by email, proves possession of the inbox. A login without 2FA is therefore usually one factor, no matter how many screens it has.
  • A factor that can be recovered by email is not a second factor. If a lost authenticator app can be replaced by clicking a link in your inbox, an attacker with access to the inbox can do the same. Real 2FA needs a recovery route that is stronger than email: recovery codes, a second registered device, or a person (admin, helpdesk) who verifies your identity. This is true for both options; they differ in who handles recovery.

docs.title: Second factor types
docs.text: Type Notes Passkeys / WebAuthn (device biometrics, security keys) Bound to the website's domain, so they can't be phished on a look-alike page. The strongest common option. TOTP (authenticator apps, 6-digit codes) Widely supported, but can be phished: a fake login page can ask for the code and use it immediately. SMS Better than nothing, but vulnerable to SIM swapping.

docs.title: OIDC claims
docs.text:
An OIDC provider returns an ID token with claims about the login. The ones that matter here:

Claim Meaning iss + sub The provider (issuer) and the user at that provider. Together they are the user's identity. email + email_verified The email address, and whether the provider confirms the user owns it. auth_time When the user last actually authenticated (not when the token was issued). Used to check freshness. amr Authentication methods used, such as pwd, otp, mfa. Standardized names exist, but providers decide which values they send and when. acr The level of the login, e.g. a level-of-assurance URI. Institutional federations (including SURFconext) often signal 2FA through acr instead of amr.

docs.title: Step-up and freshness
docs.text: Step-up authentication means asking an already logged-in user for a fresh second factor before a sensitive action, such as creating an API key or changing roles. With an OIDC provider, the server sends the user back to the provider with max_age (re-authenticate if the last login is older than N seconds), and then checks auth_time and the 2FA claim in the new token itself. The server must check this itself, because providers don't always enforce what was requested. For instance, Keycloak had a vulnerability (CVE-2026-97176) where a token could be issued at a lower level than requested.

docs.title: Threats
docs.text: Threat Description T1. Stolen password or inbox The most common attack. Any real 2FA stops it. T2. Email reassignment Old email addresses get reassigned, especially institutional ones. Our safeguards exist for this. T3. Compromised or misconfigured provider A breached provider, a careless admin, or weak account recovery at the provider. The provider can then issue valid tokens for any user. T4. Phishing A fake login page captures credentials and one-time codes. T5. Lockout A user loses their second factor. Not an attack, but recovery procedures are a common attack surface themselves.

docs.title: Option A: the OIDC provider handles 2FA
docs.text:
How it works

  • The OIDC provider requires 2FA, and signals it in the ID token. Which claim counts as 2FA is configured per deployment with OIDC_MFA_CLAIM (e.g. amr containing mfa, or a specific acr value).
  • For sensitive actions, the server checks the claim and auth_time, and redirects to the provider with max_age if the login is too old.
  • Teams without a suitable provider can use our shared OIDC provider (ZITADEL, with 2FA) for servers without sensitive data.
Pros Cons The standard pattern. Auditors, university IT and other developers recognize it immediately. The 2FA signal differs per provider. Each provider needs to be checked and configured (see Provider support). No 2FA code in our software. Enrollment, factor storage, phishing-resistance and rate limiting are the provider's job. Teams need a provider with 2FA. Free and simple providers often lack it. Our shared provider covers servers without sensitive data. Recovery is handled by the provider. With an institutional provider, the institution's helpdesk handles lost factors. The provider is a single point of trust (T3). A compromised or misconfigured provider can issue tokens that claim 2FA was used. One login prompt. Users whose institution already requires 2FA are not asked again. We can't see the quality of the 2FA. The token says 2FA was used, not whether it was a passkey or SMS, or how the factor can be recovered. Works with our existing OIDC code. Changing providers needs a migration. Account linking makes this manageable.

docs.title: Option B: our own second factor (local broker)
docs.text:
How it works

  • Next to AmCAT or AnnoTinder, the server runs a small OIDC provider of its own (a local broker), e.g. at domain.com/oidc.
  • The broker uses an upstream OIDC provider (e.g. Auth0, Google, an institutional provider) only to verify the user's email address: the first factor.
  • The broker enforces its own second factor (passkeys, TOTP) that can't be reset by email, and sends the same 2FA signal (amr, auth_time) to the apps.
  • For AmCAT and AnnoTinder the broker is just another OIDC provider: they use it as their OIDC_HOST.
Pros Cons Works with any upstream provider that verifies email, including free ones. An extra component that every deployment runs, and that we either adopt or build and maintain. The second factor is independent of the upstream provider (T1, T3). A compromised upstream provider or hijacked inbox is not enough for sensitive actions. Every deployment handles recovery. Each server needs an admin who can verify users and reset factors. We know the quality of the 2FA (e.g. phishing-resistant passkeys, T4). Two login prompts for users whose institution already requires 2FA. Changing the upstream provider is invisible to the apps. They only see the broker's iss and sub; the broker links the new upstream login to the existing identity. Less familiar. It deviates from the common pattern, so it needs explaining to auditors and colleagues.

docs.title: Existing tools
docs.text: Some OIDC providers can act as such a broker, for instance Rauthy (upstream login providers, passkeys and TOTP, lightweight). At the time of writing Rauthy is pre-1.0, and its upstream provider support is described as beta.

docs.title: Precedents
docs.text:
Option A is the common pattern, but option B also has precedents:

  • NIST SP 800-63C-4 (US federal guidelines for federated login). At its highest assurance level (FAL3), the relying party must verify that the user controls an authenticator in addition to the provider's assertion. This can be a bound authenticator that the relying party manages itself, and the provider never sees. NIST presents this as extra protection against a compromised provider (T3).
  • GitLab (self-hosted). Users can sign in via external providers, and GitLab can enforce its own 2FA on top. Administrators can choose to skip GitLab's 2FA for specific providers they trust.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: A: provider handles 2FA B: local broker Follows the common pattern Yes No Security-critical code we maintain None The broker (adopted or built) Provider requirements 2FA and a usable 2FA signal Verified email only Cheapest setup with real 2FA Our shared provider, or a free plan with 2FA (e.g. ZITADEL Cloud) Any free provider plus the broker Stolen password or inbox (T1) Protected Protected Compromised or misconfigured provider (T3) Not protected Protected for sensitive actions Phishing (T4) Depends on the provider's factors Protected with passkeys Account recovery (T5) The provider (e.g. institution helpdesk) Each deployment's admin Changing providers Migration (account linking or re-claiming) Invisible to the apps Prompts for users with institutional 2FA One Two

docs.title: Why B can be added later
docs.text:
Option B doesn't require changes to AmCAT or AnnoTinder. Both apps only talk OIDC to whatever OIDC_HOST points to, and check the same 2FA claim. A local broker is just another OIDC provider. So:

  • We can build A now, and add B later as an extra deployment option.
  • A and B can be used side by side: a deployment with a good institutional provider uses it directly (A), a deployment with a simple provider puts the broker in front of it (B).
  • Account linking and the identities table, which we need for A anyway, also cover moving a deployment from A to B.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Start with option A, and consider option B later.

  • A is the standard approach, and keeps 2FA, account recovery and phishing-resistance with providers that are managed by security teams.
  • A requires the least security-critical code in our products.
  • A's main weakness, that teams without a suitable provider would have no 2FA, is covered by our shared provider for servers without sensitive data.
  • B solves problems that A can't (provider compromise, providers without 2FA), but adds a component to maintain. Because B can be added without changing the apps, we don't need to decide on it now.

We should reconsider B when:

  • teams report that they can't get a suitable provider with 2FA,
  • a lightweight OIDC provider that supports upstream login with its own enforced 2FA reaches a stable release (e.g. Rauthy 1.0), or
  • passkeys become the default login at the providers our users rely on.

docs.title: Provider support for MFA signals
docs.text:
Checked in November 2026. Provider behaviour changes, so re-check before relying on a row.

Provider MFA signal Step-up Notes Google (consumer and Workspace) amr (mfa, hwk, swk, pwd, ...) max_age Part of the Sign in with Google "security bundle". Google includes amr only when the information is available, so it may be absent even when requested. Microsoft Entra ID amr (mfa only when MFA was completed) Conditional Access, max_age Since 2026, amr can be added as an optional claim to v2.0 tokens. Configure per app. Auth0 amr contains mfa Actions + acr_values The free plan has no step-up MFA factors (TOTP from the Essentials plan, WebAuthn from Professional). amr can be missing on silent SSO renewal. Authentik amr (pwd, mfa, passwordless WebAuthn) max_age, prompt=login acr is a fixed value, so MFA can't be requested on demand. MFA must be part of the authentication flow. Keycloak acr (levels of authentication mapped to flows) acr_values, max_age Always check the returned acr yourself (see CVE-2026-97176). ZITADEL amr and acr in the ID token max_age (to verify) The exact amr values need to be verified; one report mentions amr as a string instead of a list, so accept both. SURFconext (Dutch institutions) acr with a SURFsecureID LoA value acr_values 2FA via SURFsecureID, which institutions procure separately.

docs.title: Installation guide: authentication
docs.text:
This guide is for teams that host AmCAT or AnnoTinder themselves. It covers choosing and setting up an OIDC provider. For what our software does with the provider, see the Authentication standard.

There are two options:

  1. Our shared OIDC provider. Free, for servers without sensitive data, such as teaching and pilots.
  2. Your own OIDC provider. Required for sensitive research data. Ideally your institution's identity provider, but there are other options.

You can start with option 1 and migrate to option 2 later.

Whichever option you choose, your team is responsible for the personal data on your server. We provide a privacy statement template to get started.

docs.title: Option 1: our shared OIDC provider
docs.text:
To make it easy to start, the Societal Analytics Lab offers a shared OIDC provider (ZITADEL) with 2FA. It is open to anyone hosting our software, and separate from the identity provider for the lab's own infrastructure (see Lab authentication). You create your own organization there, and manage its users yourself. Other organizations at the shared provider can't see or manage your users.

TODO: URL of the shared provider (self-hosted or ZITADEL Cloud, to be decided).

Setting up your organization

  1. Register your organization at the shared provider's sign-up page (<shared-provider-url>/ui/login/register/org). The account you register with becomes the organization owner.
  2. In your organization's login settings, require a second factor for all users (passkey or authenticator app).
  3. Create a project with a web application for your server, using the authorization code flow, with the redirect URI of your server. TODO: redirect URI per app (AmCAT, AnnoTinder).
  4. Configure your server with OIDC_HOST, OIDC_CLIENT_ID and OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET from the application, and OIDC_MFA_CLAIM=amr:mfa TODO: verify the exact amr value ZITADEL sends. See Configuration.
  5. Invite your users. They create an account in your organization and set up their second factor.

Terms

  • No sensitive research data. Names and email addresses of users (e.g. students) are personal data too, so you are responsible for handling those according to your institution's rules.
  • Best-effort availability. If the shared provider is down, nobody can log in to your server. Keep this in mind for teaching and exams.
  • You handle account recovery. Your organization's owner can reset users' second factors. The lab does not provide a helpdesk.
  • The lab operates the provider. As the operator, the lab could in principle access every organization. This is one of the reasons the shared provider is not for sensitive data.

Is your server getting used for research data?

If you start using sensitive research data, move to your own OIDC provider first (see the Migration guide). The web client shows server admins a Shared OIDC provider: not for sensitive data label as a reminder.

docs.title: Option 2: your own OIDC provider
docs.text:
The provider must meet three requirements: it verifies email addresses, supports 2FA and signals it to our server, and supports step-up (max_age and auth_time). Which provider fits depends on your institution and on what you want to do.

Your institution's identity provider (recommended for research data)

The safest choice is a provider that is managed by a security team and has a helpdesk for account recovery. For most universities that means the institution's own identity provider. Talk to your IT department: they decide which providers may be used for research data, and they may already have one available.

SURF (Dutch institutions)

Dutch universities and research institutes are usually connected to SURF, which offers two relevant services. Both are arranged through your institution, not directly with SURF.

  • SURFconext is the standard login for Dutch institutions. Your institution's SURFconext contact connects your server as a service. 2FA is provided by SURFsecureID, which institutions procure separately, and is signalled with an acr value (OIDC_MFA_CLAIM=acr:<SURFsecureID LoA>).
  • SURF Research Access Management (SRAM) is designed for research collaborations, including members from other (also international) institutions via eduGAIN, and guests via eduID. SRAM makes sure every user logs in with 2FA: it uses the home institution's 2FA when available, and its own second factor otherwise. SRAM offers OIDC. TODO: verify which claim SRAM uses to signal 2FA.

SURF is only available to Dutch institutions. Institutions in other countries often have a comparable national research and education federation; ask your IT department.

ZITADEL Cloud free plan (small teams)

If your institution can't offer a provider, you can create your own ZITADEL Cloud instance. The free plan includes 2FA and passkeys, and lets you choose an EU data region, but is limited to 100 daily active users. We only recommend it if you don't expect many active users, or are able to move to a paid plan when you do. As with our shared provider, you handle account recovery yourself.

Other providers

OIDC Provider 2FA 2FA signal (OIDC_MFA_CLAIM) GDPR Compliant Cost Ease of Setup Notes SURFconext (Dutch institutions) Via SURFsecureID (procured by the institution) acr:<SURFsecureID LoA> Yes Institutional Medium See SURF above. Microsoft Entra ID Yes amr:mfa (add amr as optional claim) Yes Paid (Institutional) Hard (Admin setup) Proper enterprise/institutional contracts and DPAs. Google Workspace Yes amr:mfa Yes Paid (Institutional) Hard (Admin setup) Google only includes amr when the information is available. Test before relying on it. Auth0 paid plans Yes (TOTP from Essentials, WebAuthn from Professional) amr:mfa Yes Paid Easy Includes enterprise agreements, SLAs, and DPA. ZITADEL (Cloud or self-hosted) Yes amr:mfa (verify) Yes (EU region or hosting) Free plan (100 daily active users) / paid plans / hosting cost Easy (Cloud) / Medium (self-hosted) Organizations with their own admins. Self-hosted Authentik Yes amr:mfa Yes (when hosted on-prem/EU cloud) Hosting cost / labor Medium MFA must be required in the authentication flow (Authentik can't be asked for MFA on demand). Self-hosted Keycloak Yes acr:<value> Yes (when hosted on-prem/EU cloud) Hosting cost / labor Medium Map the acr value to a level of authentication that requires 2FA.

A self-hosted provider is only as secure as its maintenance: someone has to keep it updated and handle account recovery.

Not suitable:

  • Auth0 free plan. No step-up MFA factors.
  • Google consumer accounts (@gmail.com). No institutional agreements, and amr is not always present.

The 2FA signal column was checked in November 2026; details and sources are in Provider support for MFA signals. Provider behaviour changes, so test the setup before going live.

docs.title: Checklist for your own provider
docs.text:
• The provider is approved by your institution for the data on your server.
  • The provider returns email_verified: true for your users.
  • 2FA is required (or can be requested) for your users, and OIDC_MFA_CLAIM matches the provider's signal.
  • Step-up works: performing a sensitive action (e.g. creating an API key) after more than AUTH_STEP_UP_MAX_AGE seconds asks for 2FA again.
  • It is clear who handles account recovery for your users (a helpdesk, or your own admin).
  • The server admin page shows no hardening warnings.
  • If you are moving from our shared provider or another provider: follow the Migration guide.

docs.title: Migration guide: changing OIDC providers
docs.text: This guide is for teams that move their AmCAT or AnnoTinder server to a different OIDC provider, for instance from our shared OIDC provider to their institution's provider. The person hosting the server is responsible for the migration.

docs.title: Why migration needs care
docs.text:
The OIDC provider is the source of truth for the identity of a user. Our software identifies users by the combination of iss (the provider) and sub (the user at that provider), not by email address (see IBAC). A new provider means a new iss and new sub values, so without a migration the server will not recognize existing users, and all their roles are lost.

There are two strategies:

Account linking JIT re-claiming How users keep their account They link their new login while still logged in with the old one They log in with the new provider and re-claim their account via their email address Relies on email No Yes Both providers needed Yes, during a transition period No Effort for users One extra login during the transition period None Best for Servers with important data, including moving from our shared provider while it is still available Servers without sensitive data, or when the old provider is no longer available

docs.title: Account linking
docs.text:
Account linking is the industry standard way to migrate. A user can have multiple login identities (see the identities table in IBAC), so a user can add their new login to their existing account. Because the user is authenticated at both providers when linking, email plays no role.

Steps

  1. Register your server at the new provider, and check it against the checklist.
  2. Move the current provider settings to the OIDC_PREVIOUS_* variables, set the new provider in the OIDC_* variables, and choose an end date in OIDC_PREVIOUS_UNTIL (e.g. three months ahead). See Configuration.
  3. Users can now log in with either provider. Users who log in with the old provider are asked to link their new login: they sign in at the new provider, and the server adds the new identity to their account.
  4. Remind users before the end date. Server admins can see which users have not linked yet.
  5. After OIDC_PREVIOUS_UNTIL, the old provider is no longer accepted. Remove the OIDC_PREVIOUS_* variables. Users who did not link can still re-claim their account (see below).

docs.title: JIT re-claiming
docs.text:
With JIT re-claiming, the server forgets the old identities, and users re-claim their account based on their verified email address, using the same JIT account claiming mechanism we use for invitations.

Steps

  1. Register your server at the new provider, and check it against the checklist.
  2. Set the new provider in the OIDC_* variables.
  3. TODO: admin command that removes all identities, turning existing users into shadow users that can be claimed by email.
  4. Users log in with the new provider. If their verified email address matches an existing user, they claim that account.

Risks

Re-claiming relies on email ownership. Someone who controls a user's email address at the new provider (for instance after an address was reassigned) can claim that user's account and roles. Our safeguards limit this: email verification is required, roles of dormant users are disabled, and unclaimed accounts expire after 3 months. But the risk is not eliminated, so prefer account linking for servers with important data.

For a server without sensitive data (e.g. a teaching server) this is usually acceptable. It is also the fallback for users who missed the account linking transition period.

docs.title: Authentication standard
docs.text:
All software developed by the Societal Analytics Lab (AmCAT, AnnoTinder) uses the same approach to authentication. This page is the standard: what our software does, and what it requires from the OIDC provider. For deployers, see also:

  • Installation guide: choosing and setting up an OIDC provider.
  • Migration guide: moving to a different OIDC provider.
  • Two-factor authentication: where should it live?: why 2FA is handled by the OIDC provider, and what we could add later.

docs.title: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
docs.text:
OIDC is an open standard for authentication that builds on top of the OAuth 2.0 protocol. It allows clients to verify the identity of users based on the authentication performed by an external identity provider (IdP). By using OIDC, our software does not handle user authentication directly, but delegates it to an external OIDC provider. This is an industry standard, because it outsources the hard part of authentication to a dedicated provider, which is often better equipped to handle it than the application itself.

Our software works with any OIDC provider that meets the provider requirements. The person hosting our software chooses the provider, and is responsible for making sure it is suitable. The safest choice is a provider that is managed by a security team and has a helpdesk for account recovery. Talk to your institution's IT support circle.

docs.title: Choosing an OIDC provider
docs.text:
There are two options. Both require 2FA; they differ in who manages the provider, who handles account recovery, and which data is allowed. See the Installation guide for details.

Option 1: our shared OIDC provider Option 2: your own OIDC provider For Servers without sensitive data, such as teaching and pilots Any server, required for sensitive research data Provider ZITADEL, run by the lab. Teams create their own organization and manage their own users. Ideally your institution's identity provider (see the Installation guide) Maintained by The lab, with best effort A security team (recommended) Account recovery The admin of your own organization at our provider The provider's helpdesk (recommended) Cost Free Depends on the provider

Why our shared provider is not for sensitive data

  • No security team. Nobody ensures the provider is always up to date. If it is compromised, your data is at risk.
  • The lab could access your data. As the operator, the lab could in principle log in as any of its users. This will not fly with your institution's security team and data stewards.
  • No helpdesk. If a user loses their second factor, your own organization admin has to help them.

Names and email addresses of users (e.g. students) are personal data too, so any server must be used according to your institution's rules. Moving from our shared provider to your own is a migration.

The server recognizes our shared provider by its issuer (OIDC_HOST). When it is used, the web client shows server admins a Shared OIDC provider: not for sensitive data label. This can't be turned off. For other providers, the person hosting the server is responsible for choosing a provider that fits the data.

There is no option without 2FA. For development on a local machine there is a separate development mode.

docs.title: OIDC provider requirements
docs.text:
All three requirements are strict: they can't be disabled.

Requirement What the provider must do Email verification Return "email_verified": true in the ID token. Our software uses email addresses to assign roles (see Authorization). 2FA with a usable signal Support 2FA, and signal in the ID token that it was used. Providers do this differently (amr containing mfa, or a specific acr value), so the claim is configured with OIDC_MFA_CLAIM. See Provider support for MFA signals. Step-up Honour the max_age parameter (re-authenticate if the last login is older than N seconds), and return auth_time in the ID token.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Proposed names; to be aligned with the AmCAT and AnnoTinder code.

Variable Required Description OIDC_HOST yes Issuer URL of the trusted OIDC provider. OIDC_CLIENT_ID yes Client ID registered at the provider. OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET yes Client secret registered at the provider. OIDC_MFA_CLAIM no Which claim counts as 2FA: amr:mfa (default) or acr:<value>, e.g. acr:http://test.surfconext.nl/assurance/loa2 for SURFconext. AUTH_STEP_UP_MAX_AGE no Maximum age in seconds of the last 2FA login for sensitive actions. Default: 600. OIDC_PREVIOUS_HOST, OIDC_PREVIOUS_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_PREVIOUS_CLIENT_SECRET, OIDC_PREVIOUS_MFA_CLAIM no The previous OIDC provider, only during a migration. OIDC_PREVIOUS_UNTIL no Date after which the previous provider is no longer accepted. AUTH_DEV_MODE no Enables development mode. Refused unless the server only listens on localhost.

docs.title: Two-factor authentication (2FA)
docs.text:
For sensitive actions (e.g. creating API keys, changing roles) our servers require a 2FA login that is at most AUTH_STEP_UP_MAX_AGE seconds old (step-up authentication).

  1. The server checks OIDC_MFA_CLAIM and auth_time in the ID token.
  2. If the claim is missing or too old, the server redirects the user to the OIDC provider with max_age.
  3. The server checks the new ID token itself, because providers do not always enforce what was requested.

Account recovery (e.g. a lost phone) is the responsibility of the OIDC provider.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
Our software also supports direct API access via API keys. These are application-managed tokens that are decoupled from the OIDC provider.

  • API keys can only be created and changed by the main web client, in a session that passed step-up authentication.
  • API keys always have a limited scope.

docs.title: Server hardening warnings
docs.text:
The web client shows server admins a list of warnings for things that make the server less secure:

Warning Meaning Shared OIDC provider The server uses our shared OIDC provider, and must not hold sensitive data (see Choosing an OIDC provider). No 2FA signal Recent logins did not contain the configured OIDC_MFA_CLAIM, so sensitive actions are blocked. Check the provider's 2FA settings and OIDC_MFA_CLAIM. Migration not finished OIDC_PREVIOUS_HOST is still configured after OIDC_PREVIOUS_UNTIL.

docs.title: Development mode
docs.text: AUTH_DEV_MODE lets developers run our software on their own machine without an OIDC provider, logged in as a local admin. The server refuses to start in development mode unless it only listens on localhost. Development mode is never used for servers that other people use.

docs.title: For developers
docs.text:
All software developed by the Societal Analytics Lab follows these rules, to ensure consistency and security across our software stack.

Rule Details Same origin The server and web client are always hosted on the same domain. Server-side OIDC flow The server initiates and completes the OIDC flow with the trusted provider (OIDC_HOST), and sets a signed, http-only session cookie. One session per application When AmCAT and AnnoTinder are hosted together, each is a separate OIDC client with its own session. The second login completes without user interaction, because the user is already signed in at the provider. Logging out is per application. Authorization on the server The server decides what users may do, not the OIDC provider (see Authorization). API keys for other clients Other clients (e.g. R or Python) can only access the backend via API keys. Email verification The server checks the email_verified claim. This cannot be disabled. 2FA and step-up The server checks OIDC_MFA_CLAIM and auth_time for sensitive actions, and performs step-up authentication if needed (see Two-factor authentication). This cannot be disabled outside development mode.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: Authorization is based on roles. A role can be given to a specific user (IBAC), to users with a certain attribute (ABAC), or both.

docs.title: Role table
docs.text: Column Description role What role a user has (e.g. READ, WRITE, ADMIN). context The context in which the role applies (e.g. project, server). user_id If not null, the role is linked to a specific user (see IBAC). email_domain If not null, the user's verified email must have this domain (see ABAC). Can be combined with user_id to require both. require_email If user_id and email_domain are null: whether any user gets the role (false), or only users with a verified email address (true). granted_at When the role was granted (created, updated, or restored).

docs.title: Identity Based Access Control (IBAC)
docs.text:
IBAC is the primary mode of authorization: roles are given to registered users.

The identity is iss + sub, not the email address. An email address is not a unique identifier, because it can change over time: users can change email addresses, and old email addresses can be reassigned. We do use the email address as a human readable way to assign roles (e.g. giving a colleague access to a project in AmCAT). This is safe, because the role is not assigned to the email address itself, but to the user (iss + sub) that currently owns it. Changing email addresses is the responsibility of the OIDC provider: when the email for an identity has changed, the server updates the user table.

Any user that signs in is registered, optionally with a form that collects additional information. We use this for security logs and rate limiting, which is legitimate under GDPR. Email addresses add some accountability, especially when roles require an email domain.

User table

Column Description id Unique user ID. email Email address of the user, from the most recent login. has_mfa Whether the most recent login contained the 2FA signal (OIDC_MFA_CLAIM). registered_at When the user first signed in. NULL for shadow users until the account is claimed (see JIT account claiming). last_login_at When the user last signed in. reactivated_at First login after 1 year of inactivity. ... Optional user details (e.g. added on registration).

Identities table

Column Description user_id The user this identity belongs to. iss Issuer of the OIDC provider. sub Unique subject identifier at the OIDC provider. linked_at When the identity was linked to the user. last_login_at When the user last signed in with this identity.

Normally a user has one identity. A user can have more than one during a migration to a new OIDC provider.

docs.title: JIT account claiming
docs.text: Just-In-Time (JIT) account claiming lets us give roles to an email address that is not yet registered. The role is given to a new shadow user, which only has an id and email (registered_at is NULL, and there is no identity yet). The current owner of the email address is invited to claim the account and role. This can be an actual invitation, or just happen automatically when they first sign in. Claiming adds an identity and sets registered_at.

docs.title: Safeguards against email reassignment
docs.text:
Two safeguards prevent giving a role to a previous or future owner of an email address. A role is not given to a user if one of these conditions is true:

Dormant users. A role is disabled when:

role.granted_at < user.reactivated_at AND NOT user.has_mfa
  • Why: without 2FA, the OIDC provider only verifies current ownership of the email address. So after a year of inactivity, roles granted before reactivation are disabled. With 2FA required this should be rare, but it remains a safeguard for accounts claimed via email and providers that report 2FA inconsistently.
  • Restore: per role (e.g. an AmCAT project ADMIN refreshes granted_at), or by a server admin.

Expired invitations. A role is not given when:

user.registered_at > role.granted_at + INTERVAL '3 months'
  • Why: a role given to an unregistered email address must be claimed within 3 months, so that a future owner of the address can't claim it. Roles granted after registration are not affected, because then granted_at is later than registered_at.
  • Unclaimed invitations: a shadow user that is still unclaimed (registered_at IS NULL) has an expired invitation when now() > role.granted_at + INTERVAL '3 months'.
  • Restore: remove the invitation, or restore it by updating granted_at.

docs.title: Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC)
docs.text:
ABAC is the secondary mode of authorization: roles are given based on user attributes from OIDC claims. We currently only use the email domain, because this keeps the role of the OIDC provider restricted to authentication and email verification. In the future we could include other attributes (e.g. eduPerson claims from institutional providers).

IBAC and ABAC serve different purposes:

IBAC ABAC Based on Identities, tied to specific users Attributes, properties of users that can change Use Users keep their roles when they change email addresses. Important for long-term projects where researchers change institutions. Give and take away access based on a user's current situation, such as their affiliation with an institution.

Email domains are useful for:

  • Convenience: give access to anyone with an institutional email address, instead of giving everyone individual access. This should have limited privileges (never ADMIN).
  • Security: restrict access to a trusted institution. Combined with IBAC, access is restricted to a trusted person who also has a verified email address at that institution.

docs.title: Lab authentication
docs.text:
Status: open decision.

This page is about authentication for the lab's own infrastructure: our own AmCAT and AnnoTinder servers, and the AuthWall in front of services without their own login (Whisper, Ollama). It is not about the shared OIDC provider that we offer to other teams. That one runs on ZITADEL, and is kept separate from the lab's own identity provider, because it is open to the public.

docs.title: What we need
docs.text:
• Meets our Authentication standard: verified email (email_verified), a 2FA signal (amr/acr), and step-up (max_age, auth_time).
  • Forward auth for services without their own login (the AuthWall).
  • External collaborators: researchers from other institutions, including abroad, and guests without an institutional account.
  • Little maintenance, and a clear route for account recovery.

docs.title: SURF Research Access Management (SRAM)
docs.text:
SRAM is SURF's service for research collaborations. We register our services, create a collaboration (e.g. "Societal Analytics Lab"), and invite members. Members log in with their own institution (VU, or other institutions worldwide via eduGAIN), or with eduID if they have no institutional account. The VU already uses SRAM, for instance for Yoda.

  • Strengths
    • Institutional logins, including international collaborators and guests, without managing accounts ourselves.
    • 2FA for everyone: SRAM uses the home institution's 2FA when available, and its own second factor otherwise.
    • No identity provider to maintain, and account recovery goes through the user's institution, eduID or SURF.
  • Weaknesses and open questions
    • Depends on the VU: we may need to request a collaboration, and service registrations are reviewed.
    • Each service needs a privacy policy and an acceptable use policy (AUP) URL. Drafts: privacy statement and AUP.
    • Less control: we can't reset a member's 2FA ourselves.
    • To test: does SRAM's ID token include email_verified, a 2FA signal (amr/acr), and auth_time, and does it honour max_age? If SRAM enforces 2FA but doesn't signal it, our standard needs a way to handle that.

docs.title: ZITADEL (lab instance)
docs.text:
The same software as our shared provider, but as a separate instance for the lab (on its own VM).

  • Strengths
    • One software stack for both the lab and the shared provider.
    • Full control, including account recovery and 2FA resets.
    • Signals 2FA via amr (to verify).
  • Weaknesses
    • We maintain it ourselves: updates, backups, availability.
    • External collaborators need an account with us, unless we set up federation with SURFconext or eduGAIN, which is extra work.
    • No forward auth built in: the AuthWall needs oauth2-proxy (see below).

docs.title: Authentik (current setup)
docs.text: Our current lab identity provider. It has forward auth built in (proxy provider) and can serve LDAP. But since we run ZITADEL for the shared provider anyway, keeping Authentik for the lab means maintaining two identity stacks. So we only keep Authentik if we decide against both SRAM and a lab ZITADEL instance.

docs.title: The AuthWall
docs.text:
• With SRAM or ZITADEL: Caddy forward_auth with oauth2-proxy, which handles the OIDC login and session for services without their own login.
  • With Authentik: Authentik's built-in proxy provider (forward auth).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
1. Test SRAM on its acceptance environment (acc.sram.surf.nl): register a test service, log in, and check the claims in the ID token against our standard.
  2. If SRAM meets the standard (or the gaps can be handled), use SRAM for the lab, and run ZITADEL only for the shared provider.
  3. Otherwise, set up a lab ZITADEL instance on a separate VM, and migrate the lab's few Authentik users.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• SURF Research Access Management (SURF wiki)
  • SRAM at the University of Twente (incl. eduGAIN and eduID)
  • VU Research Support Handbook: SRAM invitations and eduID
  • SRAM setup guide (service registration, collaborations)
  • Authentik proxy provider
  • ZITADEL with oauth2-proxy

docs.title: Acceptable use policy: Societal Analytics Lab services
docs.text:
Draft

This is a draft, to be reviewed before use. Items marked TODO still need to be filled in or confirmed.

Version: draft, November 2026

This acceptable use policy (AUP) applies to everyone who uses a service operated by the Societal Analytics Lab: the lab's AmCAT and AnnoTinder servers, Whisper, Ollama, and the shared OIDC provider (see services covered). By using these services, you agree to this policy.

It does not apply to AmCAT or AnnoTinder servers hosted by other teams. Those teams set their own policies.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The services are provided for research and education. Use them only for these purposes, and in line with the rules of your own institution.

docs.title: Your account
docs.text:
• Your account is personal. Don't share it, or your API keys, with others.
  • Protect your password and your second factor (passkey or authenticator app). Keep your recovery codes in a safe place.
  • Report a lost second factor, a leaked API key, or any suspected misuse of your account immediately to TODO: lab contact email, or to your organization's admin for the shared OIDC provider.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
• Only upload data that you are allowed to use, and handle it according to the agreements that apply to it (e.g. your data management plan, licenses, and consent of research participants).
  • As a project admin, you are responsible for who you give access to your project's data.
  • Servers that use the shared OIDC provider must not hold sensitive research data (see Choosing an OIDC provider).

docs.title: Not allowed
docs.text:
• Using the services for anything illegal, or in violation of the rights of others.
  • Trying to access data, accounts or systems that you have not been given access to.
  • Circumventing or testing security measures without permission from the lab.
  • Disrupting the services, or using them in a way that prevents others from using them (e.g. excessive automated requests).
  • Using the shared GPU services (Whisper, Ollama) for purposes unrelated to research or education. TODO: fair use limits, if any.

docs.title: Logging and monitoring
docs.text: To keep the services secure, we log logins and actions (see the privacy statement). These logs are used for security, for investigating incidents, and to enforce this policy.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: If this policy is violated, we may suspend or remove accounts, API keys or access to projects, and inform your institution. Serious violations may be reported to the authorities.

docs.title: Availability
docs.text: The services are provided with best effort, without guarantees about availability or data loss. Keep your own copies of important data.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: Questions, and reports of misuse or security problems: TODO: lab contact email.

docs.title: Privacy statement template for self-hosted servers
docs.text:
This template is for teams that host AmCAT or AnnoTinder themselves. The team hosting a server (or its institution) is responsible for the personal data on that server, and should provide its own privacy statement. Adapt this template to your situation, replace everything in [brackets], and have it checked by your institution's privacy officer.

Our own privacy statement for the services the lab operates can serve as an example.

docs.text:

docs.text:

docs.text: TODO: to be confirmed by the VU privacy officer. Most likely, the processing of account data and security logs is necessary for the performance of a task in the public interest (education and research, GDPR article 6(1)(e)), or for the legitimate interest of securing our services (article 6(1)(f)).

docs.title: Research data
docs.text:
AmCAT and AnnoTinder store data that users upload to research projects. That data may contain personal data (e.g. social media posts or interview transcripts). For this data:

  • The research project (or its institution) is responsible for having a legal basis and the required agreements, such as a data management plan or a data processing agreement.
  • The lab processes the data only to provide the service, and only as instructed by the project.
  • Project admins decide who has access to the project's data.

TODO: confirm with the VU privacy officer whether a standard processing agreement is needed for projects from other institutions.

docs.title: Shared OIDC provider
docs.text:
The lab offers a shared OIDC provider for teams that host our software themselves. For accounts at this provider:

  • The lab processes account data (name, email address, login and 2FA settings, security logs) to provide the login service.
  • Each organization at the provider is managed by its own owner, who invites users and can reset their second factor.
  • The team hosting a server that uses the shared provider is responsible for that server, and for the data in it.

docs.text:
Recipient Why The login provider (e.g. SURF, or ZITADEL for the shared provider) Logging in. The login provider has its own privacy statement. TODO: hosting providers (e.g. SURF for SciCloud) Hosting our servers

We do not sell personal data, and do not share it for advertising. TODO: confirm that no data is transferred outside the EU/EEA (relevant if the shared provider runs on ZITADEL Cloud).

docs.text: Data Retention Account data As long as the account is active, and TODO: period after the last login Security logs TODO: period (e.g. 6 or 12 months) Research data As agreed with the research project Whisper and Ollama inputs and outputs TODO: e.g. deleted after processing, or after a fixed period Backups TODO: backup retention period

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• All traffic is encrypted (HTTPS).
  • Sensitive actions require two-factor authentication (see the Authentication standard).
  • API keys are stored hashed.
  • Servers are backed up daily to a university NAS.

docs.title: Your rights
docs.text: You have the right to access, correct, and delete your personal data, to restrict or object to its processing, and to receive your data in a portable format. Contact us at TODO: lab contact email. If you are not satisfied with how we handle your request, you can contact the VU data protection officer, or file a complaint with the Dutch Data Protection Authority (Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens).

docs.text: We may update this privacy statement. The version and date are shown at the top of this page, and the history of changes is available in the repository of this documentation.
